title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic’s Clark tells policymakers
full_text:

By David Lawder
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company’s internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act.
Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery.
He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion".
Clark’s remarks come as the company prepares for an initial public offering expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion.
HUMANS IN CONTROL, FOR NOW
Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control.
"We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials.
AI was a major topic at the IMF and World Bank meetings, as both a source of growth offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash.
Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind.
But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic’s "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants.
More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said.
STRICTEST CONTROLS ON BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH
Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology.
"Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said.
Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety."
Despite some recent high-profile incidents where rogue AI systems have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years."
Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

full_text:

By Suzanne McGee and Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss
PROVIDENCE, Rhode Island/NEW YORK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A sharp decline in CoreWeave’s bonds this week is emerging as a test of investors’ willingness to keep financing the massive buildout of AI infrastructure, as rising borrowing costs and scrutiny of debt-funded expansion hit the sector.
Analysts and portfolio managers said the selloff in the data center operator’s debt carries more significance than a concurrent rout in its shares because it may signal a broader reassessment of the risks tied to financing AI projects that may take years to generate revenue.
CoreWeave bonds issued in June at a yield of 9.675% have plunged in value, sending their yield to 15% this week.
"CoreWeave is absolutely the canary in the coal mine" for a market segment that is coming under more stress, said Max Frumes, global head of distressed and leveraged finance at 9fin, a fintech corporate credit data and analytics company.
"This is going to be a turning point in the pricing and availability and structure of credit that’s supporting the AI boom," said Frumes, who believes that other AI-linked debt will follow CoreWeave into distressed territory. "It’s going to get more expensive. There will be a lot more scrutiny and probably some pushback from investors."
CoreWeave shares fell 15.1% from Monday’s open through Thursday’s close, despite a 6% gain on Thursday after a vote of confidence from partner Nvidia. The decline was broadly in line with weakness in other so-called neocloud companies such as Nebius and Iren.
Credit investors said they already are becoming more selective.
"We’re definitely taking another look at our exposures across the AI infrastructure space, particularly where the risks are concentrated and whether we’re being adequately compensated for taking them," said John Han, a portfolio manager at fixed-income asset management firm F/m Investments.
F/m’s portfolio contains unsecured CoreWeave bonds in one of its exchange-traded funds, but only because they make up part of the index tracked by the ETF. At their current yields those bonds "certainly deserve another look," Han said. He generally prefers to invest in high-yield securities via special purpose vehicles that may offer lower yields but also more collateral and less risk.
"The market is being very selective and really singling out anything that has more leverage, and (that may be) in a bit more challenging operating environment," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager of fixed income at Catalyst funds.
To Holzenthaler and other investors, what the markets are witnessing now is an overreaction as sentiment shifts from being overly upbeat to downright bearish.
In June, the risks driving the selloff -- the sheer size of the funding needs, the leverage, the reliance on outside financing, the risk that the GPUs (graphics processing units) being purchased for data centers would be obsolete before the new facilities could open -- were merely overlooked or downplayed.
"A few months ago, I would have said people were just too optimistic around AI," Holzenthaler said.
Deutsche Bank global head of macro and thematic research Jim Reid sees the market entering a new phase in which debt financing is becoming increasingly important.
"As we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Reid wrote in a recent report. "AI financing costs aren’t dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges."
Vanguard bond portfolio manager Brad Collins said assessing AI-related debt has become more challenging as issuers bring increasingly large and varied offerings to market, often forcing investors to make decisions in days or even hours.
Rising inflation has pushed financing costs higher overall and fueled concern about what lies ahead for mammoth AI capital spending plans. Then there is the growing political controversy surrounding the construction of data centers.
Even one of the tech sector’s stalwarts allows that the road ahead may be bumpy at times. Dan Ives, partner and technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, an investment firm, estimates that 5% to 10% of planned projects ultimately will not be built.
"The growing noise around data center permitting and midterm rhetoric on power prices has given investors another reason to step back," Ives said.

The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.

"It’s a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter.. There is no basic services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive Director of the World Food Program WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
"These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I’ve been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs $450 million over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
"We tell the world now is this is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," said Skau.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Fabhalta in 2023 for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, a rare blood disorder. The drug has since received approval for two kidney diseases: IgA nephropathy and C3 glomerulopathy.

Take a look at ProPick AI’s new dividend strategies
This story comes up again and again on Reddit’s r/dividends forum.
You open a stock screener, filter for companies that pay a dividend and sort by yield, highest first. The top row shows a yield of 9% or 10% while most of the page sits at 3% or 4%. You recognize the company, see that it has paid a dividend for years, and buy their stock. A few weeks later it announces a smaller dividend, and the share price drops the same morning. The income you bought is gone, and so is part of the money you paid for it.
In July 2026, one investor described putting $18,000 into a stock yielding 9%, only to see the dividend cut two months later.
His conclusion, in his own words: “I can clearly not just sort by yield and buy what looks juicy.”
It happens to household names too
In August 2025, Charles Schwab looked at 21 years of data, 2004 to 2025, on the dividend payers among the 1,000 largest US companies.
Among the 10% with the highest yields, 24% of companies had cut their dividend. Among the 10% with the lowest yields, the figure was 4.5%.
Every company in the following table had paid a dividend for years before the change, and each gave a reason when it announced the cut: saving cash, paying down debt, or an industry downturn.
The table shows what happened to $10,000 put into each company the day before the announcement. Most of these cuts came out alongside weak quarterly results, so the price move reflects the whole announcement, not the cut alone.
| Company | Yield before the cut | Yearly income on $10,000 | The $10,000 a day later | 
|---|---|---|---|
| General Electric | about 4.5% | $430 before, $36 after (cut 92%, October 2018) | $9,120 (-9%) | 
| Kraft Heinz | about 5% | $520 before, $333 after (cut 36%, February 2019) | $7,250 (-28%) | 
| Intel | about 5.5% | $560 before, $192 after (cut 66% in February 2023, then suspended in August 2024) | $9,770 (-2%) | 
| Dow Inc. | about 9% | $920 before, $460 after (cut 50%, July 2025) | $8,250 (-18%) | 
| Campbell’s | about 6.5% | $660 before, $423 after (cut 36%, September 2026) | $9,300 (-7%) | 
Two ways to read a 9% yield
Dividend yield is a simple formula:
Dividend yield = Annual dividend per share ÷ Share price
So there are two ways to get a high yield.
The dividend can grow, which is the story you hope for.
Or the share price can fall, which gives the same number for the opposite reason. If a share price halves and the dividend stays the same, the yield doubles, and the stock moves up the screener while the business behind it is getting weaker.
A screener sorted by yield cannot tell those two cases apart, and in several of the cases in the table above, the yield had climbed because the share price had been falling.
So we built a stock list that looks beyond the yield
Rock Solid Dividends is the newest strategy in ProPicks AI, Investing.com’s AI-picked stock strategies.
Like every ProPicks AI strategy, it is run by a machine-learning model trained on years of market and financial data, backtested before it launched, and re-run on a fixed schedule. Every stock on the list comes with the reasons it is there.
You wanted a cow that gives milk for decades, not the fullest udder on the day you looked, so we built a list that checks the cow before it checks the milk.
For dividend stocks the model produces three readings for every company and combines them into one score.
- An estimate of total return, meaning the share price and the dividends counted together.
- A risk reading: how closely the company’s numbers resemble those of companies that fell hard in the past, which is the pattern behind most dividend cuts.
- The dividend yield itself, weighted so that a high yield helps a stock but never decides on its own.
There is no pass-or-fail gate. Every stock is ranked on the combined score, the top of the ranking becomes the list, and the list is rebuilt every quarter from the latest financial data, so a company whose numbers weaken slides down and out at the next rebuild.
What our AI checks on every dividend stock
Behind those three readings sit 45 metrics, checked for every dividend-paying stock.
In plain terms, before the yield counts for anything, the model asks whether the company makes enough money to pay the dividend, whether it carries too much debt, whether it has paid steadily in the past, and whether the business is growing or shrinking.
Yield is one of the 45 and carries extra weight, because this is a dividend strategy, but it never decides on its own.
The table below covers all ten areas and names every metric.
| Area | What the model asks about each company | The metrics (45 in all) | 
|---|---|---|
| The dividend itself | How big the yield is, and whether the dividend is paid out of the cash the business actually generates. | Dividend yield; free cash flow yield; payout ratio on free cash flow; payout ratio on earnings | 
| Price | Whether you are overpaying: the share price against the company’s profits, book value, cash flow and sales. | Price to earnings; price to book; price to free cash flow; enterprise value to sales | 
| Quality of the business | How much profit it makes from its assets, how wide its margins are, and how steady its valuation has been. | Return on assets; return on assets without leverage; gross margin; revenue per dollar of assets; steadiness of the P/E over 12 months | 
| Debt | How much it owes, how easily it covers the interest, and how many years of profit it would take to clear the debt. | Interest coverage; operating cash flow against capital spending; debt to equity; debt to EBITDA; debt to capital | 
| Calm or wild share price | How much the share price swings from month to month; dividend investors usually want the calm ones. | 12-month volatility of monthly returns; 12-month volatility of six-month returns | 
| Price direction | Whether the shares have been rising or falling over the past six months and year, and how close they sit to their 52-week high. | Six-month return; one-year return; distance from the 52-week high | 
| Size | How large the company is; bigger companies tend to have steadier payouts and are easier to trade. | Market value | 
| Growth | Whether sales and profits are growing, because a dividend that never grows loses value to inflation. | Revenue growth; net income growth; 12-month trend in net income; 12-month trend in revenue; 12-month trend in gross margin | 
| Track record | How many years it has paid a dividend, whether the dividend grew, and how steady cash flow and profits have been over the last two years. | Dividend streak (consecutive years as a payer, up to five); dividend growth against a year ago; free cash flow stability over eight quarters; earnings stability; net debt; how often gross margin improved over eight quarters; cash behind reported profit (accruals) | 
| Combinations | Pairs of the above judged together, so a high yield only scores well when the dividend is also well covered and the price is not collapsing. | Yield with low volatility; yield with free cash flow cover; yield with earnings cover; yield squared; yield with price direction; low volatility with price direction; cash cover with low volatility; yield near the 52-week high; both payout ratios under 100% | 
1 model, 9 markets

What else is new: Making strategies easier-to-follow
Many of you told us the high rotation of added and removed stocks each month made the AI-picked strategies hard to follow and maintain. So we changed how the AI decides when to drop a stock.
Previously, even a fractional change in the score our AI gave to each stock every month could lead to it being removed from the list. Now, the AI will only remove a stock from the list if the negative change in score is more significant.
The result is cutting the monthly stocks rotation by half, with no statistically significant change in returns in our backtests. That makes it easier for you to follow and maintain the full list of stock picks for every strategy.

A parade of tech-sector earnings this week could provide more color on the trajectory of runaway AI expenditures.
Highlighting the earnings schedule is Meta Platforms, which will report after the closing bell on Wednesday. Over the last month, the Facebook-owner has taken large strides in the race to harness AI, thanks to a well-received release of its new Muse AI model.
Muse amassed millions of downloads after the product was launched in September, underlining demand for its various services, including help with booking travel and setting up small business tools. title: Trump geothermal lease sale collides with planned Nevada solar farms
full_text:

By Nichola Groom
Oct 19 (Reuters) - The US Interior Department’s sale of geothermal leases in Nevada this week will include thousands of acres overlapping major planned solar projects from NextEra Energy and other developers, according to federal documents.
On Tuesday, the Interior Department’s Bureau of Land Management is scheduled to auction 83 parcels totaling 265,691 acres to geothermal developers. NextEra, the world’s largest owner of solar and wind generation, asked the agency earlier this year to "remove, defer or reconfigure" three proposed geothermal parcels.
President Donald Trump’s administration has promoted geothermal energy as a source of always-on electricity while largely excluding wind and solar from a broad effort to accelerate federal permitting.
In comments submitted to the agency during review of the sale, NextEra said the parcels in question overlap roughly 6,000 acres, or about 60%, of its planned 1,000-megawatt Sawtooth Energy Center in Nye County, Nevada.
BLM declined NextEra’s request in August, saying federal lands are managed for multiple uses.
Maps published on the BLM website in August show overlaps involving six proposed geothermal parcels and four major planned solar developments in the Nevada desert. One parcel, which overlaps entirely with NextEra’s Sawtooth project, did not appear on the auction website and appeared to have been recently removed from the sale.
NextEra, based in Juno Beach, Florida, said in its comments that the overlap could "create a foreseeable conflict" with its pending application.
"NextEra must collaborate with any potential lessee and adjust its operations accordingly to avoid land use conflicts," the agency said. BLM added that if NextEra’s project is approved first, it would have the "senior right" and a geothermal development would have to avoid impacts on its project.
Another solar developer, Dallas-based Leeward Renewable Energy, said a geothermal parcel overlaps about 735 acres of its proposed Lone Mountain solar project in Esmeralda County.
It urged the agency to recognize the overlap "and the non-exclusive nature of any future geothermal lessee’s development rights."
The agency added a description and maps of the overlapping projects to its sale documents. They include the proposed 300-MW Nivloc solar project being developed by Invenergy and Arevia Power’s 1,500-MW Gold Dust solar project.
Along with Lone Mountain, those projects were part of the Esmeralda 7 development, a proposed complex of seven solar farms on 62,000 acres. BLM canceled the environmental review for the complex in 2025 but said the projects may reapply for federal approval individually.
NextEra, Leeward and BLM did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Dimon flagged the possible risks to the economy from current global conflicts. The Iran war, which began in late February, has rattled financial markets, sent oil prices soaring, and sparked fears of inflation-driven central bank interest rate hikes. Meanwhile, the Ukraine war has now lasted longer than World War I.
“[T]hese wars develop in a way that you don't expect, and they can cause huge disruption to populations, to who allies with who, and obviously it's the world economy,” Dimon said.

Oct 19 (Reuters) - KKR was hit with EU antitrust charges on Monday, alleging it misled regulators during their review of its €22 billion acquisition of Telecom Italia’s fixed-line network two years ago, exposing the US buyout group to a potentially hefty fine.
The decision by the European Commission, the EU competition enforcer, followed a year-long investigation. It approved the deal in 2024, but opened an investigation a year later following complaints by other operators.
The rivals argued that prices for them to access TIM’s fixed broadband network had been unilaterally increased after the deal, even though KKR had convinced the Commission that it would not have the power to deteriorate conditions for wholesale access.
The EU antitrust watchdog said it sent a charge sheet, known as a statement of objections, to KKR for providing incorrect or misleading information about whether it would keep its existing long-term access agreements under the same terms unless mutually agreed otherwise with the third-party operators.
KKR said it strongly disagreed with the Commission’s assessment.
"We stand by the accuracy of the information provided during the Commission’s 2024 review of the NetCo acquisition. We will vigorously challenge these preliminary allegations in our response to the Statement of Objections, while continuing to engage constructively with the Commission," a KKR spokesperson said.
"The Statement of Objections is not a final finding of infringement, and the Commission’s existing clearance of the transaction remains valid."
The company can defend itself at a closed hearing in the coming months before the Commission issues a final decision.
The Commission had cleared the Telecom Italia deal due in part to the long-term agreements between FiberCop, which is Telecom Italia’s last-mile grid unit, and telecoms companies Fastweb and Iliad.
Companies found guilty of misleading regulators during reviews of their deals risk fines of up to 1% of their aggregate annual worldwide turnover.
The Commission has in recent years handed out hefty fines for such violations.

By Sudip Kar-Gupta and Elizabeth Pineau
PARIS, Oct 19 (Reuters) - France’s central government asked some local authorities to impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but not a state of emergency. But he said it was more appropriate for now to apply partial and localised curfews, without providing details.
"My determination to restore order is absolute," he told reporters. Ariel Weil, the Socialist mayor of central Paris, said on BFM TV he favoured a curfew.
Marseille banned gatherings and demonstrations. French unions meanwhile called for a new round of strikes and rallies on November 5.
The weekend of looting and violence between some protesters and police followed weeks of student demonstrations, rocking France six months ahead of its next presidential election and highlighting pressures from a weak economy and surging debt.
MINISTER BLAMES FAR LEFT
Lecornu blamed far-left groups for some of France’s worst unrest in years. "There is, after all, a far-left movement that wants to cause — we can’t put it any more strongly — profound unrest in the country in the run-up to the presidential election," he said.
Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon urged him to provide evidence. "Otherwise, he should apologise, keep quiet and stop fanning the flames of unrest," he said on X.
The Federation of Trade and Retail said almost 3,000 shops had been affected over the weekend.
"Once again, the retail sector finds itself on the front line, at a time when it is already weakened by a succession of crises," it said.
"Behind every ransacked shop are business owners, employees and families who have seen years of work and effort wiped out in a matter of hours," it added, calling for social security and tax relief for affected businesses.
Lecornu said the government would provide furlough measures from Tuesday.
Standing before a boarded-up shopfront, Gerard Nouchi, manager of two clothing stores in Marseille, said there weren’t enough police to stop the looters.
"They trashed everything, broke things, insulted us,” Nouchi said. "It was like a real tornado."
The government ordered platforms selling looted goods to take down announcements and collaborate to prosecute resellers, Junior Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff wrote on X.
Some 2,400 people were arrested and one protester died from a cardiac arrest on Saturday while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the Interior Ministry.
’LEFT WITHOUT PROTECTION’
French assets were underperforming broader European markets on Monday, though moves were more contained than at some other moments of recent political friction.
Tensions in President Emmanuel Macron’s fragile government over apparent security shortcomings — coming as the government needs to pass a budget bill to rein in its finances — could further unsettle investors.
Macron’s office said on Monday he had turned down his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez’s offer to resign, telling him instead to put an end to barricades and looting and be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings".
Nunez told reporters that Tuesday evening’s Champions League soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona would go ahead as planned.
The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon said in a joint op-ed in the newspaper Liberation that they were used to demonstrations and protests.
"But on Saturday ... for the first time, we had the feeling that whole sections of our cities had been left without protection," said the mayors, all from the centre-left.
The start of school holidays on Monday may provide relief, but students were staging more gatherings and blockades in some places, including the Louvre gallery and Sciences Po university in central Paris.
LUXURY BOUTIQUES DAMAGED
At the weekend, hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest over what many say are declining and dysfunctional public services.
At the Place Vendome in Paris, home to luxury hotels and boutiques, most shops were shuttered and surrounded by security guards on Monday. The front door of a Dior boutique was smashed, while windows belonging to other luxury brand stores in central Paris, including Rolex, Louis Vuitton, Ralph Lauren and Gucci, were damaged.
In Marseille, Ligue 1 club Olympique de Marseille said its official store on the city’s historic main avenue had been looted, while a town hall in central France was torched.
France deployed 60,000 police and other security forces on Saturday, Nunez told France Inter radio, but he acknowledged that was not enough to control violent crowds.
Cost-of-living issues also drove weekend protests in other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania.
European governments have advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution.
As France was busy cleaning up its streets, Macron arrived in Kuwait for a Gulf trip aimed at securing additional petrol and diesel supplies to bring down pump prices.

title: University of North Carolina settles federal probes by Trump administration
full_text:
S&P rises and Nasdaq jumps over 1%, rebounding after their worst week since June
By Kanishka Singh and Andrew Hay
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration has reached a settlement deal with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to close 18 federal probes over alleged race discrimination and antisemitism at the university.
Trump has targeted universities with probes and funding-suspension threats over pro-Palestinian protests against US ally Israel’s assault on Gaza, diversity initiatives, transgender policies and climate programs, leading to free speech, due process and academic freedom concerns.
The voluntary settlement agreement released by both parties does not require a monetary settlement payment and will remain effective until the end of 2028. UNC did not admit to any wrongdoing or liability and the deal maintained its eligibility for federal funding.
The agreement said UNC will appoint an internal administrator and establish a coordinator position in its compliance office to address discrimination, including antisemitism. The agreement asks UNC to provide mandatory antisemitism training to students, faculty and staff.
The university said Elizabeth Hall, associate vice chancellor for university compliance, was appointed to serve in both roles while being the point of contact for the Justice Department and overseeing UNC’s reporting obligations under the deal.
The agreement prohibited face masks or coverings concealing an individual’s identity during protests. It said student groups "shall be subject to discipline for antisemitic discriminatory conduct."
Trump has alleged pro-Palestinian protesters are antisemitic and support extremism.
Protesters, including some Jewish groups, say opposing Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories and its assault on Gaza is not antisemitic and advocacy for Palestinian rights does not imply supporting extremism.
A former Justice Department attorney said in a whistleblower complaint in August the Trump administration’s probes of universities over antisemitism accusations lacked evidence and had predetermined outcomes.
The settlement deal said UNC will adopt and maintain "non-discriminatory" admissions policies and "not use any racial proxy."
It does not prevent UNC from considering how applicants overcame adversity at a personal level and it may consider facets of family background like poverty if those considerations are applied consistently, the deal said.
The Justice Department said that on a quarterly basis, UNC will send any antisemitism and race discrimination complaints it has received to the US Justice and Education departments.
The Supreme Court rejected affirmative action at colleges in 2023 when it struck down race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and UNC.
Trump has cracked down on diversity initiatives, casting them as discriminatory against white people and men. Civil rights advocates say they help marginalized groups like ethnic minorities, LGBT communities and women.
The government has also settled with some other schools.
Last year, Columbia University agreed to pay more than $200 million to the government to resolve probes and Brown University said it would pay $50 million to support local workforce development under a settlement.
Harvard has yet to make a deal.
